149.s: Most were from Birmingham and stayed together; he still keeps in touch.
149.ch: Band family, war years and wrap-up
149.q: Yes. Well, most of us were from the same hometown and then we went to two different schools. Tuggle Institute I went to with Cap Sims and Bob Range. Then, the rest of the band, they was at Industrial High School, which was a few blocks apart. So, when we met up and originated the band in college, we

149.t: Enjoyment and no resentment among sidemen
149.s: He says no one resented him and the men stayed with him.
149.ch: Band family, war years and wrap-up
149.q: And the, and the thing about the boys, the enjoyed seeing me doing it. They felt good about it and had fun. They enjoyed seeing me do it. And we'd just kid each other about this or that.

929.t: Getting along in a band; Albert Warner and Sonny Henry
929.s: DeVore says a band with bad feeling cannot play well, and mentions the unspoken closeness of Albert Warner and Sonny Henry.
929.ch: Band building and learning from musicians
929.q: Oh absolutely. Yeah. Not only from the musical and from the philosophy and that's just as important as anything else. I mean being able to get along with your fellow man that seems to be the most important thing of all. When there's a bad feeling running in the band you're not going to play as good…

570.t: Why the New Orleans bands stick together
570.s: Russell and Penn discuss how loyalty and lack of arguments make Thomas's band play well together.
570.q: Mr. Bill, I've heard other musicians say when we be out together sometime that Thomas has got a bunch of men that never augurs, have no trouble on the bandstand like some bands usually do, and we don't.

499.t: Stuff's chemistry and Gordon Edwards's football analogy
499.s: Everyone in Stuff respected each other's turf; Gordon Edwards likened the band to a football team and the members supported each other offstage.
499.q: Yeah. Everybody in that group was very cognizant — to borrow your word — of what the other guy was playing and nobody was like suppressing their ego especially but everyone wanted — Gordon always equated it with a football team. You know everybody’s got a job to do, you’re the safety, you’re the…

104.t: Jimmy's generosity in letting her grow, and the Metropole band
104.s: Jimmy was her biggest booster and never jealous, letting her expand even if they worked apart; they combined on quartet gigs in Detroit while he played the Metropole with Joe Sullivan and Pee Wee Russell.
104.q: In retrospect, the more I think of Jimmy being, having a great deal of pride in what I could do, and . . . He has always been my biggest booster. It seemed like it was really generous of him to not be jealous or be saying, “Woman, you stay at home” or “Forget piano playing,” like some people would.…

677.t: The band should have been incorporated
677.s: They remember a brotherly, immaculate band that took care of each other and regret it changed.
677.q: Yeah, long time, but there's one thing I always say, that if there's a band in the country that should've been incorporated, --

146.t: A brotherly band: Rushing stingy, Walter Paige and Hot Lips Page
146.s: The band chipped in for each other except Jimmy Rushing; Walter Page and Hot Lips Page were unrelated and spelled their names differently.
146.q: Oh, he just liked the boys. That was a band more brother-like. The guys out there were all good to each other. If a guy got broke and he wanted to borrow some money or they got hungry and needed some money, they'd all chip in and let him have some.

90.s: Late breakfasts, late movies and visits from musicians like Bob Mitchell; he calls it a highlight of his career.
90.q: This band was pretty much like a family. In fact, quite a few nights...practically every night after we finished work, we would go down on the corner to a place where we would eat breakfast and sit around and rap, and the other musicians would come...called cookers(?). The other musicians would…

232.t: Fair treatment of sidemen; Basie Gibbens remembers
232.s: He never had violence with his men; Basie Gibbens recalls that men said Fields was fair.
232.q: Yeah, but you know, that's one thing that I can say, out of those thirty or thirty five years, as many different characters that I worked with, I got along with them pretty nice.

73.t: The band as a happy family
73.s: The band got along despite varied personalities and had a ball.
73.ch: Inside the Basie rhythm section and band family
73.q: We were just like -- with all the different personalities we were just like a happy family.
